sources_considered.why: Altman's own statement of the scaling notion Marcus refers to.
Shows the size of OpenAI's compute commitments, which bears on 'bet the company'.
A prominent researcher doubts further scaling, which partly supports 'wrong'.
Google DeepMind says scaling pre-training still gave large gains, which cuts against 'wrong'.

receipt.public_excerpt: It appears that you can spend arbitrary amounts of money and get continuous and predictable gains; the scaling laws that predict this are accurate over many orders of magnitude.

evidence_items.explanation: Confirms the view Marcus attributes to Altman. It does not show whether the view was wrong.

receipt.public_excerpt: We are looking at commitments of about $1.4 trillion over the next 8 years,” he wrote.

evidence_items.explanation: About $1.4 trillion in compute commitments against roughly $20 billion in annualised revenue shows a very large bet on compute. This fits 'bet the company' loosely, but it does not show the bet was wrong.

receipt.public_excerpt: But is the belief that if you just 100x the scale, everything would be transformed? I don’t think that’s true.

evidence_items.explanation: A leading researcher doubts that more scale alone will transform AI. That is an opinion, not a measurement showing the scaling laws failed.

receipt.public_excerpt: Contra the popular belief that scaling is over—which we discussed in our NeurIPS ’25 talk with Ilya Sutskever and Quoc Le—the team delivered a drastic jump. The delta between 2.5 and 3.0 is as big as we’ve ever seen. No walls in sight!

evidence_items.explanation: Google DeepMind's Gemini co-lead says scaling pre-training still gave large gains in late 2025. This cuts against the claim that the scaling view had been shown wrong.

unresolved_gaps: No independent measurement up to the post date shows that capability stopped following the scaling relationship Altman described.
'Wrong' has no agreed test. Experts disagreed in late 2025 (Sutskever vs. Google DeepMind).
Whether OpenAI bet its 'entire' company on scaling, rather than mostly on it, is a matter of degree.
